en.question: A workflow receives 90 requests per hour requiring qualified human approval, but its active reviewers can process only 30. A trained reserve can add 80 per hour. Policy forbids execution without approval, permits deferral, and requires notice when the 15-minute service target cannot be met. Which two responses preserve meaningful review under this overload? Select 2 answers.

options.text: Bound admitted work, keep unreviewed actions pending or safely deferred, and notify users when review will miss the service target.
options.note: Admission and pending-state controls prevent the growing queue from becoming an implicit bypass. Communication handles the service miss without redefining unreviewed work as approved.

options.text: Automatically execute requests waiting more than 15 minutes, marking their review records for next-day retrospective approval.
options.note: A timeout is not a qualified decision, and retrospective review cannot satisfy approval before execution. This protects a latency metric by violating the mandatory control.

options.text: Activate the qualified reserve with the same evidence, rejection authority, and escalation process, then monitor capacity and review quality.
options.note: Additional qualified capacity can exceed the stated arrival rate without weakening the review contract. Maintaining evidence and authority avoids replacing review with untrained throughput.

options.text: Treat historical reviewer agreement as advance approval for the highest-confidence requests until the active queue falls below capacity.
options.note: Past agreement does not constitute a decision on each request that requires approval. This silently substitutes a model score for the mandated human control during peak demand.
